To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the return times between pairs of severe coral bleaching events has decreased by a factor of two since the early 1980s, from 12 years to 6 years, and that this decrease is a consequence of both the increasing intensity of El Nino Southern oscillation (ENSO) events and of the increasing global mean sea surface temperatures (SST).

(i) the median interval between severe bleaching events at 100 reefs has diminished steadily since the 1980s and now averages only six years, (ii) as global warming has progressed over this period, tropical sea surface temperature anomalies are warmer now during La Nina than they were during the 1980 El Nino event, and (iii) as a consequence, bleaching now occurs in all El Nio phases.
the return interval between severe bleaching events is shorter than it was in the past, and that the return interval has been shortening over time.
